summary: This best current practice document gives guidelines for writing definitions of new IPFIX Information Elements. It explains the conventions for elements registered with IANA and gives guidance to expert reviewers evaluating registrations.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a how-to guide for adding new words to the IPFIX dictionary, plus a checklist for reviewers.

subtitle: The rulebook for inventing new IPFIX data fields, and for the experts who decide whether they get registered.

tldr.problem: IPFIX can carry almost any network measurement, but only if each new data field (an Information Element) is defined consistently. Without rules, the IANA registry fills with duplicates and awkward definitions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets naming, data type, numbering and structure rules for new Information Elements, defines how expert reviewers (the IE-DOCTORS) approve, revise and deprecate them, and adds checklists and a compact text notation for templates.
tldr.outcome: New definitions should look like existing good ones, and nothing should be registered unless it is needed. This is a Best Current Practice (BCP 184) and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7013 is a Best Current Practice and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It remains the guidance for authors and reviewers of IPFIX Information Elements.

sections.title: Why Guidelines for Information Elements
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol is self-describing: a sender announces what each record contains using templates built from Information Elements. Because of that, defining a new Information Element is often all it takes to apply IPFIX to a new measurement or management use case.

RFC 7013 is written for two audiences: people who define new elements, and the IPFIX experts informally called IE-DOCTORS who review additions to the IANA IPFIX Information Element registry. Together with RFC 7012, it defines how that registry is managed. It does not cover changing the IPFIX protocol itself, which needs a Standards Track RFC.

The document boils down to two meta-guidelines: define new elements that look like existing ones, and do not define elements unless you need to.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX describes network traffic using a list of named fields, like a form with labelled boxes. This guide explains how to add a new box to the form without making a mess.

sections.title: Defining a New Information Element
sections.content:
An element is eligible for the registry if it is unique, has as little internal structure as possible, and is not about a proprietary or nonstandard application. A definition needs a descriptive name, a data type from the IPFIX data type subregistry, and an English description.

Names must be unique, start with a lowercase letter and use camel case, such as sourceMacAddress or destinationIPv4Address. An element tied to a protocol should name it first, like sipMethod.

Data types must match the data. Values with a natural width use the matching integer type (for example tcpControlBits is unsigned8). Counters and identifiers should be signed64 or unsigned64, with reduced-size encoding where needed. Time values need the right precision, and strings or octet arrays with length limits must state them.

Numbering: IANA assigns the lowest free identifier in the range 128-32767. Identifiers 1-127 are reserved for compatibility with NetFlow version 9. Units, data type semantics and value ranges should be given where they apply. Enumerations must point to an IANA registry or subregistry, and elements that cannot be reversed for bidirectional flows (RFC 5103) must say so.
sections.plainLanguage: A new field needs a clear name written the same way as all the others, the right kind of box (number, text, time) and a number from the next free slot. Nobody gets to reuse a name that is already taken.

sections.title: Structure, Multiplicity and Bad Examples
sections.content:
Elements with an internal structure described in their description are not recommended. The exceptions are a direct copy of a structured protocol field (such as tcpControlBits), a raw section of a packet (such as mplsLabelStackSection), tightly related flags that should always appear together, and values that refer to an external structured type such as a MIME type or URL.

Otherwise, split the idea into several simple elements. The RFC's example is an "endpoint" made of host, port and protocol: use sourceIPv4Address or sourceIPv6Address, sourceTransportPort and protocolIdentifier instead of one opaque element. For items that repeat, either list the element several times in the template, use a basicList from IPFIX Structured Data (RFC 6313), or export raw bytes as a variable-length octetArray. A new element must not encode multiplicity or order in its definition.

Some registry entries are explicitly not good models. Examples include initiatorOctets and responderOctets (duplicates of octetDeltaCount and its reverse), p2pTechnology (a three-state enumeration stored as a string) and the numbered mplsLabelStackSection family.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not cram a whole address label into one box. Give the street, the town and the number their own boxes. And do not copy old boxes that were already done badly.

sections.title: Review, Revision and Deprecation
sections.content:
Requests go to IANA, which forwards them to the IE-DOCTORS appointed by the IESG. They check compliance with the RFC, other IPFIX RFCs, and consistency with existing elements. They may work with the requester to fix a request, and in exceptional cases reject frivolous ones. They cannot overrule IETF consensus: elements added with IETF consensus need IETF consensus to be revised or deprecated. Decisions can be appealed.

Changes to existing elements are discouraged and must stay interoperable. The RFC lists the allowed kinds: fixing an obvious editorial error, correcting an ambiguity that breaks interoperability, widening a type without changing its representation (such as unsigned32 to unsigned64), adding missing information, defining a reserved value or bit, widening the permitted range, and harmonising with a corrected external reference. Each accepted change raises the element's revision number by one, starting from zero.

Anything else can only be handled by deprecation. Collecting Processes should keep supporting a deprecated element, Exporting Processes should not export it, and its name and ID must never be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: A small panel of experts looks at each request. Fixing a typo is fine, but if a change would confuse programs already using the field, the old field is retired and a new one made instead.

sections.title: When Not to Add an Element
sections.content:
The element number space is limited, and a bigger registry is harder to understand, so new entries should only be added if there is an intent to implement and deploy them. Research or experimental uses should use enterprise-specific elements, scoped to a Private Enterprise Number, as described in RFC 7011. These suit implementation-specific data, research inside one community, and proprietary information. They are also the right choice for pre-standardisation testing, and authors are advised to follow this RFC's guidelines even then.

Reuse is preferred. Changing only the context is not a reason for a new element: an HTTP extension should reuse sourceIPv4Address rather than invent httpClientAddress. By contrast, ipClassOfService (Element ID 5), ipDiffServCodePoint (Element ID 98) and ipPrecedence (Element ID 196) are all acceptable because each records how the same bits were interpreted. For timestamps, absolute ones such as flowStartMilliseconds are recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: If the dictionary already has the word you need, use it. If you are only trying out an idea, scribble it in your own notebook first and add it to the shared dictionary later.

sections.title: The Definition Checklists
sections.content:
Section 7 condenses the rules into three checklists, with items that tools could check marked "(tool support)".

  • Checklist 1 (must be met by all): unique name, never reusing a current or deprecated name; a substantially different meaning; lowercase start and camel case; data type that matches the data; appropriate semantics; a unique identifier from IANA; and a review of information leakage or misuse.
  • Checklist 2 (must be met when applicable): correct time precision; length limits noted for strings and octet arrays; enumerations tied to a registry or a new Expert Review subregistry.
  • Checklist 3 (should be met): protocol or application name first, suitable integer widths, 64-bit counters and identifiers, no internal structure or multiplicity, semantics, units and ranges defined, non-reversibility noted, and intent to deploy on production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three lists to tick off: things you always have to do, things you must do in special cases, and things you ought to do if you can.

sections.title: IESpec Text Notation and Templates
sections.content:
Internet-Drafts defining new IPFIX applications should describe each element with its description, data type, optional semantics, units and range, references and an ElementId. The ID is written as a placeholder such as TBD1 until IANA assigns it. New applications should generally not fix their templates, because that throws away IPFIX flexibility, and any recommended template should say that element order is not significant and that extra elements may appear.

To write templates compactly, the RFC defines the IESpec notation: name(number)<type>[size], with parentheses for the number, angle brackets for the type and square brackets for the size (65535 or v means variable length). Enterprise-specific elements use name(pen/number). A partial IESpec may give just a name or number, and a size there overrides the default, which expresses reduced-size encoding. A {key} context marks Flow Keys, {scope} marks scope elements, and + nests elements inside structured data.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a short-hand way to write down a field: its name, its number, its kind and its size, each in its own kind of brackets, so people and programs can read it easily.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IE-DOCTORS must weigh what new elements could reveal. They look at whether exported data contains personally identifiable information or confidential details, such as partial payload or exploitable configuration. Such elements are not forbidden, but the security risk must be balanced against the usefulness of the data.

Element-specific concerns must be written up in the Internet-Draft, or in the element's own description if there is no draft. As an example, RFC 5474 concluded that the private parameters of a hash function should not be exported in IPFIX, and the PSAMP specification (RFC 5476) says a device should not export full conversation payloads, since that would be wiretapping, and must respect local privacy laws.
sections.plainLanguage: Before adding a new field, the experts ask: could sharing this hurt someone, like revealing private information? If it could, the risks have to be written down and weighed.
